The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, and the Hollin, its steam engine since 1932, still makes the climb every morning, round curves and over rails laid along the lower valley. Higher up is the scree slope above Gessen. The stone wall that holds it back was raised by the line's builders in 1911, and this spring it has begun to bulge. The valley road runs directly beneath the same slope.

Since April the train has paused at Gessen each morning so that Ilse Marran can climb a few metres and look over the scree slope. Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, has driven painted stakes into the stone, and Ilse checks each one against the top of the wall. From the halt the scale of the slope is plain: a grey fan of loose rock rising three hundred metres, with goats grazing along its upper edge. The Hollin, which took on water at Pell, waits below with steam up.

The council has twice asked the regional government for the money to pay for a new wall, and is still waiting for an answer. Otherwise the timetable runs as it always has. The first train leaves Tarsel at dawn with the farmers' cheese, loaded there from the high farms, a trade the timetable is built around; the visitors come up later and photograph the viaduct from the windows as the train crosses the Lenn gorge. The quarter of an hour at Gessen is printed in the timetable now.

In winter the snowploughs keep the road clear, and the line runs too, so the village has two ways down. Both pass beneath that slope. If the wall gives way in some wet spring, the scree will bury the track and the road together, and the village will have no way down at all.

Each time we passed beneath the scree, I caught myself counting Tomas's stakes and hoping that every one still stood where it had stood the day before. At Tarsel the others stepped into the sun, but I stayed by the window, staring down the valley at that grey fan of stone.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Money was short. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost two-thirds as much as the next cheapest, because it left out the flood wall the others drew, though it would take two summers to build, like the rest.

So the pool has reopened with no wall. Lind had the tiles lifted and stored beneath the terrace in wooden crates, to be relaid in a few years; for now the floor of the new basin is painted blue. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the terrace above them. The café stands by the north gate, its walls lined with timber from the old changing cubicles. The swimming club, which had offered to buy the tiles one by one, has been promised them back under the water instead. The diving tower, patched at the council's expense, still stands.

On opening day Councillor Ruth Abney, who spent twenty years at the bar defending clients in the county court, cut the ribbon, and the swimming club swam the first length. The Ost slid past a few yards away.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look past the bathers at the river: it ran then exactly where it runs now. Whenever it rains for a week, I find myself checking the river gauge at Hollin Bridge.

In 2019 the Ost rose higher than anyone could remember, and it can rise that high again. If the next winter is like that one, the water will reach the crates under the terrace before anyone can move them, and the pike may be lost after all.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine. Residents voted online for paint, the parks crew chose the seven colours themselves, and Councillor Mara Varga persuaded the council to buy a thick sealing paint, the kind used on harbour walls, for concrete that has been soaking up rain since 1971.

It helps to know how the bridges are checked. Each spring the city's inspectors walk every span and read the bare concrete for hairline cracks, which show as thin dark lines after rain, and they ring each one in coloured chalk. A crack caught before water gets in is a cheap repair; mending the cracks found late has cost the city far more. The whole method depends on seeing the grey surface itself.

So far the bridges are busier than they have been in years. Visitors come down to the river with cameras, and Mr. Abeyta at the foot of the teal bridge now simmers a second pot of stock each morning for the crowds. A class at Larch Street School had sent in a scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that people could tell the bridges apart and find the right one, but the crew picked colours that would show from the station. A mix-up at the depot, which misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, held up the work for a day.

What I cannot stop thinking about is next April. The sealing paint is thick and glossy, so the inspectors will be reading colour instead of concrete, and a crack that opens under the coat this winter could stay out of sight until it has run through a railing. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green, and that plan was shelved for want of money.

I will be on the plum bridge when the inspectors come next spring, waiting with my stomach in a knot to see whether they can still find what the new coat may be hiding from them.

passage:
Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that strong riders stand on their pedals. After sixty wet winters those stones are working loose, and on race morning several rocked under my feet.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. At the bridge he offered sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale his own light bicycle in place of Jory's heavy steel one, which Jory politely declined. Before the start Arlo called the race anybody's, Jory and Nell Odrey included.

Arlo led from the stone bridge past the old chapel, and Jory passed him halfway up the Knuckle, picking a line between the loose stones, then rode on past the war memorial to the green. His winning time of 10:04 was well outside the champion's record, and Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated.

On the Friday before the race the county engineer had given Hettie a ring to report on his survey of the bend. Unless the stones are relaid by next spring, the Knuckle will be closed to the race, and relaying them costs more than the parish has. The rest of Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, and tarmac on the Knuckle would take away the very climb Kesterby rides it for. All afternoon I kept thinking that a race run every June since 1961 could lose its hill within a year.

When the handbell sounded for the last rider, I caught myself wondering whether Kesterby would hear it on Moss Lane next June, or anywhere at all.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran keeps an old machine in her hall cupboard, its booklet tucked inside the lid, though she only smiled when I asked about it. The keys had stopped working, stuck with old grease, and Dad, sure the keys would loosen, brought a can of oil from the garage that turned out to be empty. My cousin Juno said giving up now would waste a good machine, and she knew where to go.

March 4. Juno walked me to Keel Street, and Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman, greeted her by name and asked after her bicycle. He said he was seeing that model for the first time. We made a deal: he gave me a can of oil for the stuck keys, and in return I would pay him by sweeping his shop floor every Saturday in March. All he wanted besides, he said, was a clean floor.

March 5. Gran pressed each key while I oiled it; on my own I would have flooded the works. As the keys loosened, she told me how she had typed a letter every Sunday for twenty years to her brother at sea, on this very machine. The shift key still stuck, so every capital jumped half a line above the rest. The carriage spring pulled firmly, and Dad's shaving brush cleared the grease.

March 7. Gran's old ribbon is black on top and red underneath, and the lever between them had slipped halfway. When I typed my opening sentence, every letter came out half black and half red, and I typed it twice more just to watch the colours stripe across the page. Juno, trying a typewriter for the first time, typed her name in stripes too.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Afterward I found Gran's carbon copies in the back of the case, every Sunday letter to her brother. Juno, who is past the contest's age limit, read them with me and asked if she could borrow a few to read at home.
